subtype: Approach: rehearsing tough questions with peers [Action]
passage:
I'm Shankar, and the worst pitch I ever gave was to my kitchen wall, and the second worst was to two friends who actually know things. Mridul has raised money twice; the other one, Kavita, worked at a fund. Before real meetings I sat them down and said, be rude.
They asked about competition. I gave a paragraph. They asked what it costs us to win one clinic, and I fumbled. Then, why now? Mridul just said, "I'd rather you stumble here than in front of the money."
So I rewrote every answer, shorter each time, and each time cut anything I couldn't stand behind. By the third round my answers fit in one breath. I still felt shaky, but I knew what I would say.

qa.q: Who are the two friends Shankar pitched to?
qa.a: Shankar pitched to Mridul and Kavita.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when fumbling the question about the cost of winning one clinic?
qa.a: Shankar felt embarrassed and exposed, since the fumble came in front of two people who know the field.

qa.q: What could Shankar do after the third round to be sure the answers are ready?
qa.a: Shankar could pitch once more to someone new, and ask them which answer sounded least believable.

qa.q: Why might Mridul press so hard in the practice round?
qa.a: Mridul would rather see Shankar stumble in private practice than in front of real investors, as Mridul says directly.

grounding: The monologue shows a founder pitching to two experienced friends who ask about competition, costs and timing, and rewriting answers until short and honest.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing tough questions with peers [Action]
passage:
Mehak asked two of us who had raised money before to tear her pitch apart before her real investor meetings. Varun and I sat on her sofa with coffee and did exactly that.
I asked, "Who else does this, and why won't they crush you?" She talked for four minutes. Varun asked, "What does it cost you to get one customer, and what do they pay you over a year?" She guessed, then admitted she had guessed. I asked, "Why now? Why not five years ago?" Silence.
She didn't argue. She wrote every question on a card. Three evenings later we did it again. The competition answer was now three sentences. The customer numbers were real, from her sheet, including one she didn't like. For "why now" she said, "I'm not sure it's perfect timing; here's what changed last year."
I don't know how nervous she was at the real meetings. But her answers were short and honest.
— Leela

qa.q: Which question met silence the first time?
qa.a: "Why now? Why not five years ago?"

qa.q: What might Mehak have felt when she admitted she had guessed?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed and exposed, but she didn't argue; Leela can only see her writing the questions down.

qa.q: What else could Mehak do before the real meetings?
qa.a: Practise once more with someone who doesn't know the business, to check that the short answers make sense to outsiders.

qa.q: How does Leela see Mehak's second attempt?
qa.a: Leela sees real improvement: shorter answers, real numbers even when unflattering, and honesty about why now.

grounding: It shows a founder pitching to two experienced friends who ask about competition, customer economics and why now, then rewriting answers until they are short and honest.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing tough questions with peers [Action]
passage:
Thursday. Jatin pitches his EV-charging startup to Vishal and Farida, two friends who have raised money before, in Vishal's living room. Vishal asks, "What's your margin on each charge?" Jatin says, "Healthy." Farida asks, "Why won't the big fuel companies just do this?" Jatin talks for five minutes and loses his own thread.
Sunday. Jatin sits with a notebook and rewrites. Margin: the actual number, from last month's data. Competition: "They will. Our edge is housing societies they don't want to bother with." Why now: "Two state subsidies changed in March." Each answer under thirty seconds.
Tuesday, the next week. Round two in the living room. Vishal repeats the margin question. Jatin gives the number and its weakness. Farida nods. "That I believe."

qa.q: What did Jatin first say about his margin?
How did Jatin feel after losing his own thread on the competition question?
qa.a: Jatin likely felt flustered and embarrassed, which drove the careful rewriting on Sunday.

qa.q: What made the rewritten answers stronger?
qa.a: They used actual numbers, admitted weaknesses and stayed under thirty seconds.

qa.q: How does Farida react to the second round?
qa.a: Farida is convinced, saying "That I believe" once Jatin gives the real number and its weakness.

grounding: It shows a founder rehearsing with two experienced friends who probe competition, margins and timing, and rewriting answers until they are brief and honest.
